title: India Notifies Rs 1.28 Lakh Crore Semicon 2.0 Scheme to Build End-to-End Chip Ecosystem
excerpt: The government has formalized its most ambitious semiconductor policy, covering chip design to fabrication with $13 billion in incentives, minority stakes in startups, and a target of capturing 10 percent of the global chip market.
body:
• India has notified the Rs 1.28 lakh crore ($13 billion) Semiconductor Mission 2.0, covering chip design, fabrication, equipment manufacturing, and R&D to build an end-to-end domestic chip ecosystem
  • The scheme targets 50,000 to 60,000 direct jobs and aims to capture close to 10 percent of the global semiconductor market, according to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw
  • The government will take minority stakes in semiconductor startups and offer seed funding up to Rs 15 crore, with a royalty financing model requiring companies to pay back 1.5x the support received
  • Fabrication units get 40 percent capex support, compound semiconductor fabs get 35 percent, and 100 chips have been identified as strategically important for sectors from aviation to consumer electronics

India has formally notified its most ambitious semiconductor policy yet — a Rs 1.28 lakh crore ($13 billion) package called India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 that aims to build a complete domestic chip ecosystem spanning design, fabrication, equipment manufacturing, and research.

IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the scheme would position India to capture "close to 10 percent of the global semiconductor industry's market," a statement that frames the country's chip ambitions in terms of global market share for the first time.

What the Scheme Covers

Semicon 2.0 moves well beyond the first mission's focus on attracting individual fabrication plants. The new policy targets the entire value chain: chip design startups, domestic manufacturing of semiconductor equipment and raw materials, fabrication units, and dedicated R&D centres.

The government has identified 100 chips as strategically important, spanning aviation, consumer electronics, drones, and transportation. For these, the policy creates a structured incentive stack: 40 percent capital expenditure support for silicon fabrication units, 35 percent for compound semiconductor and discrete fabs as well as OLED, Micro LED, and LCD display manufacturing, and 30 percent for raw materials, wafer and substrate manufacturing, test facilities, and R&D centres.

"Close to 10 percent of global semiconductor industry's market will be in India. Larger designing firms like L&T, Cyient and Tata now have an opportunity."

— Ashwini Vaishnaw, Minister of Electronics and IT

An additional production-linked incentive of 2 to 10 percent applies to equipment and components manufacturing, layering performance rewards on top of the capex subsidies.

Startup Stakes and Royalty Financing

In a departure from traditional subsidy models, the government will take minority equity stakes in semiconductor startups, matching private investment. Chip-designing startups and MSMEs can access seed funding of up to Rs 15 crore.

The payback mechanism is equally unconventional: a royalty financing model where companies pay 5 percent of net revenue until the government recovers 1.5 times its initial support. This replaces the typical grant-and-forget approach with a self-sustaining funding cycle — if companies succeed, the government recoups more than it invested; if they struggle, the repayment burden stays proportional to revenue.

Scale Targets

The scheme sets cumulative targets of Rs 4 lakh crore in investment, Rs 2 lakh crore in production, and Rs 1 lakh crore in exports. Vaishnaw projected 50,000 to 60,000 direct jobs, with the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) estimating the policy could catalyse over Rs 5 lakh crore in private investment over five to seven years.

India has already hit one early milestone ahead of schedule: the country reached 85,000 trained semiconductor engineers in four years against an original ten-year timeline. The application window for the new scheme has no stated end date, signalling that the government intends to keep the door open as the ecosystem matures.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated tens of thousands of Indian-origin semiconductor professionals working at companies like Intel, Qualcomm, TSMC, and AMD across Silicon Valley and global chip hubs, Semicon 2.0 creates a tangible pathway back. The startup equity provisions and seed funding lower the barrier for diaspora engineers considering ventures in India, while the fabrication incentives give established firms like Tata and L&T the financial backing to build teams that could draw on global Indian talent.

The policy also opens a corridor for diaspora investment. With the government willing to co-invest as a minority stakeholder, the risk calculus shifts for NRI investors eyeing India's semiconductor space.
